chunks: Sa'd narrated from Ibrahim ibn Mahziyar, from his brother, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Muhammad ibn Hakim, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a woman whose menstruation rises (becomes irregular/ceases). He said: 'The rising of the menses is of two types: either it is a cessation due to menstruation, or it is a rise due to pregnancy. Whichever it is, she becomes permissible to her husbands if she gives birth or if three white months pass for her in which there is no blood.'

The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And it is not permissible for him to expel her from his house unless she brings about a manifest indecency. This is indicated by the saying of the Exalted: 'Do not expel them from their houses nor should they [themselves] leave [during the waiting period] unless they commit a manifest indecency.' (1) And this is a clear statement of what we said.

key_terms.الشَّيْخُ: The Sheikh (referring to the commentator, likely Shaykh al-Tusi)
key_terms.ثَلَاثَةُ أَشْهُرٍ بِيضٍ: Three white months (months of no bleeding)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a woman whose menstruation has stopped or become irregular regarding marital relations and housing rights?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Rida (AS) clarifies the ruling for women with prolonged menstruation (istihadah), establishing that marital relations resume after three consecutive months of 'white days' free from blood, regardless of whether the cause is natural cessation or pregnancy. Shaykh al-Tusi reinforces this by citing the prohibition of expelling the wife from the marital home unless she commits a 'manifest indecency' (fahisha bayyinah), linking the physical state of purity to the legal stability of the marriage. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on maintaining the marital bond and the specific criteria for distinguishing between pathological bleeding and natural cycles.
